hops.title: In the cochlea, potassium is the ion that rushes in
hops.text: The usual rule of thumb says sodium rushes in to excite a cell and potassium leaks out. Cochlear hair cells run it backward. The fluid bathing their bundles holds about 150 mM potassium and about 20 micromolar calcium, far lower than most body fluids, which leaves the pore less blocked. That fluid also sits at +80 mV relative to its neighbors, and the hair cell's interior is negative, so the total push on potassium is larger than 80 mV. In 2012, an MIT team tapped it in a guinea pig, drawing at least 1.12 nanowatts for up to five hours to run a tiny 2.4-gigahertz radio.

image.caption: The cochlea keeps a +80 mV potassium battery, real enough to run a tiny radio chip.

hops.afterHeading: The ladder: what each rung rules out
hops.title: The wasabi channel that was not the hearing channel
hops.text: TRPA1 is the channel that gives wasabi, horseradish and mustard oil their sting. In 2004, a Nature paper proposed it as a candidate hair-cell transduction channel, and the case looked good: its RNA appeared as hair cells became mechanosensitive, antibodies labeled the tips of the bundles, and suppressing it reduced hair-cell function. In 2006, two groups deleted Trpa1 in mice, one of them led by the lab that had proposed it. Both found normal hearing. One also found normal balance and normal vestibular hair-cell currents; the other found that pain-sensing neurons no longer responded to mustard oil or garlic. Location plus knockdown had pointed to the wrong channel.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A white mouse calmly sniffs a small dish of green wasabi paste next to a silver tuning fork on a wooden table.
image.caption: Mice missing TRPA1 reacted less to mustard oil yet heard normally, so location and knockdown were not enough.

hops.afterHeading: A pore inside a complex: TMIE, LHFPL5, CIB2 and a worm structure
hops.title: Why spinner mice circle and Tmc1 mice do not
hops.text: The spinner mouse was described in 1962 because it was deaf and ran in circles. In 2002 the cause turned out to be a large deletion containing Tmie, the mouse version of the gene at the human DFNB6 deafness locus. Mice lacking Tmc1 are deaf too, but they do not circle: Tmc2 fades in the maturing cochlea yet persists in balance hair cells and can stand in for Tmc1. The backup is partial. A 2024 study found these mice had lost the balance nerve's response to head acceleration and had impaired eye reflexes. And in mouse cochlear hair cells, neither TMC1 nor TMC2 forms working transduction channels without TMIE.

sources.citation: Deol MS, Robins MW (1962) Journal of Heredity 53:133-136.
